items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and describe how it forms in sodium chloride.

rubric.why: A covalent bond is defined by mutual sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as mutual sharing of electron pair(s) between atoms.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the definition; award 1 mark if the answer only mentions sharing of electrons without describing the bond between atoms.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies a single bond as one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct description.

rubric.why: Double and triple bonds involve two and three shared pairs, respectively.
rubric.description: Describes double and triple bonds by the number of shared electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each type correctly described; examples may support the answer but are not required.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms mutually share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons, for example, in H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons, for example, in O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons, for example, in N₂.

items.followUp: Define molality and derive its formula in terms of the mass of solute and solvent.

rubric.why: Molarity is defined as the number of moles of solute per unit volume of solution.
rubric.description: Defines molarity as moles of solute per unit volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: The number of moles is obtained by dividing solute mass by its molar mass.
rubric.description: Relates moles of solute to its mass and molar mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Substituting the amount of solute into the definition gives the molarity relationship.
rubric.description: Derives molarity as moles of solute divided by volume of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: The final expression and unit complete the derivation.
rubric.description: Gives the mass-based formula and an appropriate molar concentration unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct final expression or equivalent formula with suitable units.

modelAnswer: Molarity is the number of moles of solute dissolved per dm³ of solution.
Number of moles of solute, n = mass of solute (g) / molar mass (g mol⁻¹).
Molarity, M = n / volume of solution (dm³).
Therefore, M = mass of solute / [molar mass × volume of solution].
The unit of molarity is mol dm⁻³.

items.followUp: Calculate the molar mass of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄.

rubric.why: The calculation uses the atomic masses of hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen in HNO₃.
rubric.description: Shows the correct atomic masses and adds their contributions for HNO₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct setup.

rubric.why: The molar mass of HNO₃ is 63 g mol⁻¹.
rubric.description: States the correct molar mass with an appropriate unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct final answer with unit.

modelAnswer: Given: H = 1, N = 14, O = 16 g mol⁻¹.
Molar mass of HNO₃ = 1 + 14 + 3(16) g mol⁻¹.
Molar mass of HNO₃ = 63 g mol⁻¹.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of phosphorus according to shells and subshells.

rubric.why: Silicon has 14 electrons arranged as 2, 8 and 4 in its shells.
rubric.description: Gives the shell electronic configuration of silicon.

rubric.why: The subshell configuration accounts for all 14 electrons in silicon.
rubric.description: Gives the subshell electronic configuration of silicon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct configuration.

modelAnswer: Silicon has atomic number 14, so it has 14 electrons.
According to shells: 2, 8, 4.
According to subshells: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p².

items.followUp: Why does atomic size decrease from left to right across a period?

rubric.why: Each step down a group adds an electron shell.
rubric.description: States that additional electron shells are added down the group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the increase in occupied shells.

rubric.why: The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction is weaker and atomic size increases.
rubric.description: Links the added shells or increased shielding to the larger atomic size down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct cause-and-effect explanation.

modelAnswer: Moving down a group, each successive element has an additional electron shell.
The outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and experience greater shielding, so the atom becomes larger.

items.followUp: Describe how atomic size changes down a group and across a period in the periodic table.

rubric.why: Shielding increases down a group because additional electron shells are occupied.
rubric.description: Describes the increase in shielding down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend.

rubric.why: Across a period, added electrons enter the same main shell, so shielding changes little.
rubric.description: Describes shielding as nearly constant or changing only slightly across a period, with a valid reason.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend and explanation.

modelAnswer: Down a group, the shielding effect increases because each successive element has an additional electron shell.
Across a period, the shielding effect remains nearly constant or increases only slightly because electrons are added to the same main shell.

items.followUp: How does a compound differ from a mixture? Give one example of each.

rubric.why: A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition throughout.
rubric.description: Describes the uniform composition of a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct distinction.

rubric.why: A salt solution is a suitable homogeneous-mixture example; sand and water is a suitable heterogeneous-mixture example.
rubric.description: Provides suitable examples of both homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; its components are evenly distributed. Example: salt solution.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, and its components are not evenly distributed. Example: sand and water.
